definition.text: Action taken together by a group of people to improve their condition and reach a common objective.

facts.text: The economic theory of collective action concerns providing public goods through the collaboration of two or more individuals; Mancur Olson's 1965 book The Logic of Collective Action is an early analysis of public-good costs.
Olson argued that individuals with more resources carry a higher burden of providing a public good, while poorer ones tend to free ride, which can lead to under-provision.

Institutional designs for public goods include joint products that tie a private good to a public good, clubs that exclude non-members, and federated structures, since collaboration emerges more easily in small groups.
The social identity model of collective action explains participation through perceived injustice, perceived efficacy and social identity.

definition.text: Research conducted with the participation of the general public or amateur and nonprofessional researchers.

facts.text: It is used in ecology, biology, conservation, health, astronomy and more; the term first appeared in a January 1989 MIT Technology Review issue on community labs studying environmental issues.
Projects are categorized by participants' involvement; at the low end, contributory or crowdsourcing projects have citizens collect observations, offer computing power or install sensors.
Citizen science has contributed much to biodiversity analysis, mostly species occurrence, abundance and phenology data, with birds the most observed group.
Smartphones and internet platforms vastly expanded participation, through apps such as iNaturalist and Mosquito Alert.
Ethics and data governance, including data protection law and community control over reuse, are growing concerns; ECSA published Ten Principles of Citizen Science in 2015.
Researchers have estimated the monetary value of citizen science contributions, for example from seven Zooniverse projects.
